nullRationales: This narrative review reports no pooled sample, confidence interval, or single effect size for the recommendation, so n, effectSize, and ci remain null.

Both percentage bounds match the directly read abstract and Energy section.
No predicate turns this into personal bulk-rate advice.

nullRationales: This review reports an evidence gap rather than a pooled intervention effect, so n, effectSize, ci, and figures remain null.

checks: Statement says the precise surplus is unknown; it does not imply that a surplus has no effect.
It preserves the review's controlled-study limitation.
No numeric bulk-rate threshold or personal recommendation is introduced.
The abstract directly states that the specific surplus is unknown and proposed sweet spots have not been validated in resistance-training populations.
The claim preserves the evidence gap and does not infer that an energy surplus has no effect or yield a personal rate.
No pooled intervention effect, n, or CI exists for this evidence-gap claim; Grade C is appropriate.

surfacePlacementReview.directSource: Direct re-read of the Frontiers full text for 10.3389/fnut.2019.00131 (Slater et al. 2019); the 2026-08-02 claim reviews were not relied on for placement.
checks: The Introduction directly states 'the specific energy surplus required to facilitate muscle hypertrophy is unknown' and the Abstract states surplus estimates 'have never been validated in a resistance training population to confirm the sweet spot', so the claim statement is source-accurate.

Surfacing this evidence-gap fact on a bulk goal-draft computes no personal surplus, gain rate, or energy target, so it does not weaken GR-1, the deficit cap, or the intake floors (which concern deficits, not surplus).

The claim remains non-prescriptive and population-honest (citation population unstated); it asserts only that the maximizing surplus is unvalidated, not that an energy surplus has no effect, which the source explicitly disputes.

checks: Statement is limited to the 11 competitive male bodybuilders and four-week study.
The direct methods read confirms anthropometric estimation and the diet tables confirm different macronutrient distributions, so the statement does not claim an energy-only effect.
Energy intake, group sizes, muscle-mass changes, and p value match the source tables and Results prose.
PMC6942464 reports 11 competitive male bodybuilders randomized to higher (n=6) versus moderate (n=5) energy intake for four training weeks.
Table 2 confirms different energy and macronutrient distributions; Table 3 reports estimated skeletal muscle mass +2.7% versus +1.1%, with Results prose reporting p = 0.03.
Wording avoids an energy-only causal inference and identifies the estimate; Grade C reflects the very small, short single trial.

nullRationales: The directly read abstract provides no pooled effect size or confidence interval, so effectSize and ci remain null.

No claim treats short rests as ineffective or supplies a personal prescription.

Its conclusion says rests longer than two minutes seem required to maximize strength in resistance-trained individuals, while robust gains can still occur with shorter rests.
Claim is limited to trained individuals and strength, retains qualified wording and justified nulls, and Grade B fits a non-quantitative systematic review.

nullRationales: The directly read abstract provides no confidence interval or numeric effect-size estimate, so ci and effectSize remain null.

The one- versus three-minute setup and significant anterior-thigh result match the directly read abstract.
No claim turns the triceps p = 0.06 trend into evidence of a difference.
PubMed directly reports 21 young resistance-trained men randomized to one- or three-minute rests for eight weeks with other training variables held constant.
The abstract reports significantly greater anterior-thigh muscle thickness with three-minute rests; the triceps p = 0.06 trend is not promoted to a finding.
Claim retains the young trained-male, anterior-thigh, and eight-week scope; null effectSize and CI are justified and Grade B fits one controlled trial.

nullRationales: The directly read abstract provides no subgroup sample sizes, confidence intervals, or numeric hypertrophy effect size, so those fields remain null.

checks: Statement will retain young-adult, post-training-block, and maintenance-dose scope.
The one-third and one-ninth doses, 16-week block, 32-week maintenance phase, and young-adult hypertrophy result match the abstract.
No inference is made about a short deload or an individual maintenance prescription.
PubMed directly reports 70 adults, 16 weeks of three-times-weekly resistance training, then 32 weeks randomized to detraining, one-third, or one-ninth maintenance doses.
Both maintenance doses preserved phase-one muscle hypertrophy in young adults but not older adults.

entries.sourceRead: PubMed author abstract for PMID 39364857; DOI resolution checked directly with Crossref
evidenceLocations: PubMed PMID 39364857, Methods: periodic training was 10 weeks resistance training, 10 weeks detraining, then 10 weeks retraining; the comparator had 10 non-training weeks then 20 weeks continuous resistance training.

nullRationales: The directly read abstract does not give confidence intervals or numeric group effect sizes for the final comparison, so ci and effectSize remain null.
No publisher figure is stored; only source-read programme durations and participant count are retained.
entries.populationRationale: The source explicitly identifies healthy, untrained participants; the claim retains that status and does not generalize to trained lifters or a one-week deload.
entries.gradeRationale: One randomized comparison directly reports detraining and retraining in untrained adults. Grade B reflects the controlled design but its narrow population and long break.

checks: Statement will preserve the untrained population, 10-week break, retraining context, and matched 20-week continuous-training comparator.
It reports decline and regain rather than calling the break harmless.
No claim equates a 10-week detraining phase to a short scheduled deload.
PubMed directly reports healthy untrained participants randomized to periodic training (20 completers) or the comparator (22 completers), with 45% female in each group.
The periodic arm was 10 weeks training, 10 weeks detraining, then 10 weeks training; strength and VL/BB CSA declined during detraining and were rapidly regained.

The statement specifies the comparator's matched 20-week continuous-training block after 10 non-training weeks and does not equate the break with a standard deload. Grade B and null CI/effectSize are appropriate.

entries.sourceRead: Europe PMC full text for PMCID PMC10170537; DOI resolution checked directly with Crossref
evidenceLocations: PMC10170537, Methods/Participants: 38 resistance-trained females (at least six months of self-attested training) completed the per-protocol analysis; both groups completed six weeks of prescribed 25% restriction, with the intermittent group taking two one-week energy-balance breaks.

PMC10170537, Results—Laboratory Measures: no significant group-by-time interaction for body weight, percent body fat, fat mass, or fat-free mass (all p >= 0.08); the intent-to-treat body-composition findings were also non-significant (all p >= 0.09).
PMC10170537, Discussion—Strengths and Limitations: weekly set volume differed between groups even though total prescribed volume was matched, limiting causal interpretation.
nullRationales: The claim reports that this trial did not detect a body-composition difference; it does not store a comparative effect size or CI because those would not establish equivalence and are not needed for the narrow null-result record.
No publisher figure is stored; only source-read participant count, restriction amount, and programme durations are retained.
entries.populationRationale: The paper identifies resistance-trained females with at least six months of self-attested continuous training. The claim is confined to that sex and training context; the citation population is therefore trained.
entries.gradeRationale: This is one small controlled trial with substantial attrition and unequal weekly set volume between arms. Grade C and an explicit no-detected-difference statement avoid treating non-significance as evidence of equivalence or generalizing beyond resistance-trained females.

checks: Statement is confined to this trial's resistance-trained female population, six weeks of restriction, and body-composition outcome.
It reports that the trial did not detect a group difference, not that diet breaks and continuous restriction are equivalent.
The known weekly-volume imbalance and attrition are reflected in the C grade and must not be hidden by the claim wording.

PMC10170537 directly supports 38 per-protocol resistance-trained females, six weeks of continuous 25% restriction versus six restricted weeks delivered over an eight-week intermittent programme with two one-week energy-balance breaks.

Laboratory body-composition group-by-time interactions were non-significant (all p >= 0.08); intent-to-treat body-composition findings were also non-significant (all p >= 0.09). The claim says the trial did not detect a difference rather than treating the conditions as equivalent.

Weekly set volume differed despite matched prescribed total volume and attrition was substantial; Grade C, null comparative effect/CI, trained-female scope, and search-only reachability are appropriate.

entries.sourceRead: Europe PMC full text for PMCID PMC7739314; DOI resolution checked directly with Crossref
evidenceLocations: PMC7739314, Methods—Study Design/Participants: 27 resistance-trained men and women completed seven weeks of supervised resistance training while randomized to continuous restriction or five restricted days plus two carbohydrate-refeed days per week at maintenance intake.

PMC7739314, Results—Table 3: dry fat-free mass changed by -0.2 kg (95% CI -0.7 to 0.3) with refeeding and -1.9 kg (95% CI -2.7 to -1.2) with continuous restriction; the table marks a group-by-time interaction at p <= 0.001.
PMC7739314, Participants: 58 healthy resistance-trained adults were recruited, but 27 completed and were included in final analysis; training experience was self-attested.
nullRationales: No publisher figure is stored; the source-read table values and confidence intervals are retained as extracted text.

The claim deliberately excludes the paper's broader fat-free-mass and resting-metabolic-rate interpretations because the directly read table identifies the group-by-time interaction only for dry fat-free mass.
entries.populationRationale: The source enrolled resistance-trained males and females and used a mixed-sex final sample; the claim retains that mixed trained-adult scope rather than applying it to a specific sex, competitive bodybuilders, or an individual diet plan.
entries.gradeRationale: One small seven-week controlled trial directly reports the dry-fat-free-mass interaction, but high attrition and self-attested training experience constrain confidence. Grade C reflects those limitations and the narrow outcome.

checks: Statement will name the two refeed days, seven-week duration, resistance-trained mixed sample, and dry-fat-free-mass outcome only.
The stored change values, CIs, and group-by-time significance are read directly from Table 3.
Broader claims about fat-free mass or resting metabolic rate are excluded because they are not supported by the table's group-by-time results.
PMC7739314 directly reports 27 final-analysis resistance-trained adults (13 refeed, 14 continuous; mixed sex) in a seven-week randomized comparison.
Table 3 supports dry fat-free-mass change of -0.2 kg (95% CI -0.7 to 0.3) versus -1.9 kg (95% CI -2.7 to -1.2), with the table's group-by-time marker p <= 0.001.

The claim correctly confines itself to dry fat-free mass, calculated as fat-free mass minus total body water; it does not extend to broader fat-free-mass or resting-metabolic-rate conclusions. High attrition and self-attested training justify Grade C and the narrow scope.

entries.sourceRead: Direct full-text read via PMC11873903 and Firecrawl scrape; DOI displayed on the PMC article.
evidenceLocations: PMC11873903, Abstract/Methods: a three-round Delphi-type process had 17 experts rate technical complexity and eight later-round experts assess novice appropriateness, with 70% agreement required.
PMC11873903, Methods/Procedures: novice means no resistance-training experience or no training for several years, and raters were instructed to assess technical components rather than load.

PMC11873903, Conclusion/Limitations: the authors frame the list as guidance rather than doctrine; some exercises and regressions were absent, and the list was not directed at adults with chronic conditions or functional limitations.
nullRationales: This is a candidate-source record, not a drafted claim, so no source values, quote, effect size, CI, or population field is stored in a YAML record.
The study is expert consensus rather than an intervention outcome and cannot establish personal suitability, safety, or an individual exercise prescription.
entries.populationRationale: Any later claim must retain the paper's defined novice population and label its expert-consensus origin. Optional experience may rank this context but must not infer novice status from first use or hide the labelled source from another user.
entries.gradeRationale: No claim grade is assigned at intake. A future atomic claim must grade expert consensus independently of the source's exercise examples and preserve its stated limitations.
entries.nextReview: Requires claim-specific direct-source hostile reviews before any YAML drafting.

entries.sourceRead: Direct full-text read via PMC6950543 and Firecrawl scrape; DOI displayed on the PMC article.
evidenceLocations: PMC6950543, Abstract: the systematic review included 30 articles on advanced resistance-training methods and techniques.

PMC6950543, Discussion 3.1: the review describes mechanical tension as one factor in the conventional hypertrophy model and notes that high-load work emphasises mechanical tension and neural recruitment.
PMC6950543, Discussion 3.1: the review also reports that its summarized load comparisons have important volume and fatigue qualifications.
nullRationales: The source is queued only for a non-prescriptive explanation; no load, volume, rest, or failure rule is extracted into a claim because those require separate direct support and scope review.
The source uses neural recruitment language but does not by itself establish a precise motor-unit-recruitment explanation suitable for a standalone claim.
entries.populationRationale: The review spans its included studies rather than one product-relevant population. Any future claim must expose the underlying applicability rather than relabel the mechanism as universal or personal.
entries.gradeRationale: No claim grade is assigned at intake. A future mechanism claim must distinguish an explanatory model from an intervention effect and grade the direct evidence for its exact wording.
entries.nextReview: Requires claim-specific direct-source hostile reviews before any YAML drafting.

entries.sourceRead: Direct full-text read from the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid repository's author-produced post-peer-review manuscript via Firecrawl scrape; the manuscript identifies the publisher DOI and its accepted-manuscript status.
evidenceLocations: Alix-Fages et al. author manuscript, Introduction: neural drive is the sum of action potentials from active motor units and modulates force through recruitment and discharge-rate adjustments.
Alix-Fages et al. author manuscript, What Causes Muscle Growth?: mechanical tension in skeletal-muscle fibres is identified as key to the hypertrophy stimulus.

Alix-Fages et al. author manuscript, Resistance Training and Nervous System/Conclusions: motor-unit recruitment and firing activity determine produced tension, while the review calls for future work linking neural activity with hypertrophic response.
nullRationales: The full manuscript supports a cautious explanatory statement, but not a personal load, volume, failure, exercise-order, or training recommendation.

It contains no pooled quantitative result for the combined tension-and-motor-unit statement, so a future claim must leave n, effect size, CI, and figures null unless another directly read source supports them.
entries.populationRationale: The narrative review cites varied examples rather than a pooled or single study population, so any mapped claim must retain an unstated population and must not infer applicability from a selected exercise or optional experience.
entries.gradeRationale: The author manuscript is directly readable, but a future claim must reflect its narrative-review design and repeated calls for further research on neural activity's hypertrophic role.

entries.sourceRead: Direct full-text read from the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid repository's author-produced post-peer-review manuscript via Firecrawl scrape; the manuscript identifies European Journal of Applied Physiology 122 (2022), DOI 10.1007/s00421-022-04906-6.
evidenceLocations: Alix-Fages et al. author manuscript, What Causes Muscle Growth?: 'The mechanical tension produced in the skeletal muscle fibers is key for the muscle hypertrophy stimulus.'
Alix-Fages et al. author manuscript, Introduction: neural drive from active motor units modulates force through recruitment and discharge-rate adjustments.

Alix-Fages et al. author manuscript, Resistance Training and Nervous System: recruitment and firing rate determine the tension produced; Conclusions: fibre recruitment and tension depend on central-nervous-system activity.
nullRationales: This narrative review supplies no pooled participant count, quantitative effect size, confidence interval, or extractable figure for this explanatory statement, so n, effectSize, ci, and figures remain null or empty.

The claim excludes the review's practical programming suggestions and does not state that motor-unit activity alone causes hypertrophy; the review itself calls for future research on neural activity's role in hypertrophic response.
entries.populationRationale: The review does not define a pooled or single intervention population for this combined explanatory statement. Its scattered athlete, bodybuilder, and patient examples cannot be converted into a user population, so the citation is labelled unstated and the card preserves that applicability uncertainty.
entries.gradeRationale: Grade C reflects a directly read narrative mechanism review available as an accepted manuscript, not a pooled intervention effect. The source supports the physiological relationship in the statement but repeatedly treats neural activity's independent hypertrophic role as requiring further research.

checks: Direct manuscript sections support both clauses: fibre mechanical tension is key to the hypertrophy stimulus, and motor-unit recruitment/rate activity regulates force and produced tension.
The wording deliberately excludes the source's prescriptions, individual set logic, and an unsupported claim that neural activity independently causes hypertrophy.
Narrative-review design, accepted-manuscript access state, unstated population, and absent quantitative fields support Grade C with documented nulls.

The direct manuscript's What Causes Muscle Growth section calls fibre mechanical tension key to the hypertrophy stimulus; its Introduction and nervous-system discussion connect motor-unit recruitment/rate activity to force and tension.

The statement says motor-unit activity helps regulate tension rather than asserting a personal intervention, a failure/load rule, or a settled independent neural cause of hypertrophy, matching the source's future-research cautions.

Hub-empty and general exercise-selection are approved only as labelled general evidence with predicates and trigger null; unstated population and null quantitative fields remain visible rather than inferred.

entries.sourceRead: Direct full-text read from the Wiley article via Firecrawl scrape; DOI page was accessible at the checked route.
evidenceLocations: Murphy and Koehler, Abstract/Methods: the synthesis examined randomized resistance-training interventions lasting at least three weeks and compared energy-deficit with non-deficit contexts; its primary paired analysis had a limited literature pool.
Murphy and Koehler, Results 3.5: the meta-regression estimates an approximately 500-kcal/day deficit at zero predicted lean-mass change.
Murphy and Koehler, Discussion 4: matched comparisons across separate studies, population differences, and DXA protocol differences limit interpretation.
nullRationales: No goal-rate, intake target, or user-specific loss calculation is extracted: the source's meta-regression is a population model, not an individual prescription.
Existing M1 claims citing this DOI remain visibly pending-M6-review and are not silently promoted to a new surface.
entries.populationRationale: A future claim must retain the review's resistance-training and energy-deficiency eligibility limits and must not convert the model into a conclusion about a draft goal or a particular user.
entries.gradeRationale: No claim grade is assigned at intake. Any future atomic context claim must separately assess the limited paired literature and the mixed-study meta-regression design.
entries.nextReview: Requires claim-specific direct-source hostile reviews before any YAML drafting.

entries.sourceRead: Direct full-text read via PMC8365736 and Firecrawl scrape; DOI displayed on the PMC article.
evidenceLocations: PMC8365736, Abstract/Methods: this overview covers adults with overweight or obesity and summarizes exercise after weight loss, not draft maintenance-energy selection in resistance-training users.
PMC8365736, Results 3.4.4/3.5: the included evidence found no significant exercise effect on weight regain or on body-composition change during the maintenance phase.
PMC8365736, Discussion/Conclusion: the authors note only limited controlled maintenance evidence and call for more research.
nullRationales: The evidence concerns a clinically distinct post-weight-loss population and exercise intervention, not a general calorie-maintenance or lifting-goal fact.
No claim is drafted because converting this result into a maintenance-goal card would change its population, outcome, and wellness scope.
entries.populationRationale: The source applies to adults with overweight or obesity after weight loss; it must not be generalized to MyoStat users selecting maintenance.
entries.gradeRationale: No grade is assigned because this candidate is rejected for the intended surface rather than rephrased into an out-of-scope claim.
entries.nextReview: Keep the maintenance surface silent unless a directly supported, scope-matched source is found and reviewed.
